ctx-1948.prompt: Which statement correctly sums up the difference between the two 1948 texts?
options: Lasswell cares only about effect, Shannon only about noise.
Lasswell describes communication through content, channel, audience and effect questions; Shannon sets the meaning of the message aside as far as the engineering problem is concerned.
Both published the same theory in two different journals.
Shannon treats meaning as the most important problem; Lasswell studies only telephone lines.
ctx-1948.explain: The second option is correct: Lasswell’s five questions (who, what, channel, whom, effect) put content and effect at the centre, while Shannon asks how a message chosen from a set of possible messages is carried accurately, and keeps meaning out of the engineering problem. The first option is tempting because it reduces each theorist to one word; in fact Lasswell asks about the communicator, the content, the channel and the audience as well as the effect, and noise is only one component of Shannon’s subject. The third option confuses the two texts because of the words ‘1948’ and ‘communication’; their authors, fields and questions differ.

ctx-bell.prompt: Why was it reasonable for a telephone company to answer “how much information can this line carry?” independently of the meaning of messages?
options: Because engineers think meaning is always unimportant.
Because the line cannot know in advance which message will be chosen and must be able to carry every possible message; the measure is built on those alternatives.
Because telephone lines carry only meaningless sounds.
Because Hartley had proved that meaning can never be measured.
ctx-bell.explain: The correct option gives Shannon’s design reason: the system must work for every message that could be chosen, and which one will be chosen is unknown. The first option is tempting because the ‘engineer = indifferent to meaning’ cliché comes easily; but Shannon says meaning is irrelevant to the engineering problem, not unimportant; it is a division of labour, not a philosophy. The fourth option attributes to Hartley a proof he did not give: he only wrote that he wanted to eliminate psychological factors from the measure.

people-trio.prompt: Which of the following would be wrong to assume about the name “Shannon–Weaver model”?
options: The system diagram comes from Shannon’s 1948 paper.
Weaver wrote the essay that opened Shannon’s paper to the general reader.
Weaver, like Shannon, was an engineer working at Bell Laboratories.
Both texts were published in the same book in 1949.
people-trio.explain: Weaver was not a Bell Labs engineer but the director of the Rockefeller Foundation’s natural sciences division; he came in as the interpreter of Shannon’s paper. This wrong sentence circulates in some sources because of the ‘joint work’ connotation of the name. The other three options are true: Shannon draws the diagram, Weaver interprets it, and the two stand side by side in the 1949 book.

claim-lasswell.prompt: A researcher is studying under what economic and political pressures a news site puts certain stories forward. Which of Lasswell’s five questions is she working in?
options: Who? (control analysis)
Says what? (content analysis)
In which channel? (media analysis)
With what effect? (effect analysis)
claim-lasswell.explain: Studying who chooses the stories, and under what pressures, is the field of the ‘who’ question: the source that starts and steers communication, that is, control analysis. The second option is tempting because the subject is news stories; but content analysis counts and analyses what is said, not why it was put forward. Media analysis focuses on the channel itself, and effect analysis on the traces left in the audience.

claim-functions.prompt: A newspaper column discusses the government’s new decision from the viewpoint of different parts of society and contributes to the search for a shared response. Which of Lasswell’s functions is this closest to?
options: Surveillance of the environment
Correlation
Transmission of the social heritage
Entertainment
claim-functions.explain: Contributing to a shared response among different parts of society is the correlation function (Wright calls it ‘editorial activity’). The first option is tempting because the column is also about news; but surveillance is reporting a threat or opportunity, not coordinating the response. Transmission passes the heritage between generations, and entertainment is not in Lasswell’s list at all.

claim-shannon.prompt: In Weaver’s speech example (“when I talk to you…”), which box of the diagram does the voice mechanism correspond to?
options: Information source
Transmitter
Channel
Receiver
claim-shannon.explain: The voice mechanism turns the message chosen by the brain into a signal called sound pressure: the transmitter. The brain is the source, the air is the channel, and the ear with its attached nerve is the receiver. The third option is tempting because ‘sound’ travels through air; but the medium that carries it is the channel, not the apparatus that produces the sound.

concepts-bit.prompt: A friend has thought of a number between 1 and 16, all equally likely. With yes/no questions, in how many questions can you guarantee to find it at minimum?
concepts-bit.explain: 16 = 2 to the power 4; each question halves the options, so 4 questions are enough (4 bits). ‘8’ is tempting because after the first question 8 options remain and one tends to stop there; but the game does not end there. ‘16’ would be asking the numbers one by one; with good questions there is no need.

concepts-levels.prompt: A public-service spot arrives on screen intact and viewers understand what is said correctly, but their behaviour does not change at all. At which of Weaver’s levels is there a problem?
options: Level A (technical)
Level B (semantic)
Level C (effectiveness)
None; because the message was transmitted correctly
concepts-levels.explain: The symbols were transmitted correctly (A is fine) and the meaning arrived (B is fine); but the received meaning did not affect conduct in the desired way: an effectiveness problem, level C. The last option is tempting because ‘transmitted correctly’ is true for level A; but on Weaver’s map success does not end with transmission.

assumptions-shared.prompt: True or false: In Shannon’s theory, “information” is a measure of how important or meaningful the content of a single message is.
assumptions-shared.explain: False. In Shannon–Weaver theory, information is a measure not of the meaning of a message but of the freedom one has in choosing it, that is, of the set of possible messages and their probabilities. Two messages, one loaded with meaning and the other nonsense, can be equivalent as far as information goes. The ‘information = meaningful content’ association comes from everyday language and misleads readers of the theory.

how-shannon.prompt: Put a message’s journey through Shannon’s diagram in the right order.
items: The source chooses one message from the set of possible messages
The transmitter turns the message into a signal (encodes)
Noise mixes into the signal as it moves along the channel
The receiver turns the signal back into a message (decodes)
how-shannon.explain: The order follows the boxes of the diagram: the source chooses, the transmitter encodes, the channel carries and noise mixes in, the receiver decodes, the destination receives. Putting noise after the receiver is a common mistake: noise is added to the signal in the channel, before it reaches the receiver.

how-lab.prompt: In the Zimmermann telegram case, which element has no box in either diagram yet changed the course of the event?
options: The foreign minister who sent the telegram
The line the telegram travelled on
The third party who listened to the line and decoded the cipher
The receiver in Mexico
how-lab.explain: The minister is Shannon’s source and Lasswell’s ‘who’, the line is the channel, and the receiver in Mexico is the receiver and destination; all have boxes. The listening third party is not noise (noise is an unwanted distortion added to the signal; the listener adds nothing to the signal, it reads it) and it is not the receiver either; although it shaped the course of the event, it has no box in either diagram.

evidence-fields.prompt: A researcher counts which topics appear how many times on the front pages of three newspapers. Which of Lasswell’s five fields is she working in?
options: Control analysis
Content analysis
Media analysis
Effect analysis
evidence-fields.explain: What is being counted is ‘what is said’, so this is content analysis. The third option is tempting because newspapers are a channel; but media analysis examines the distinctive features of the channel (newspaper versus radio), not the counting of content that passes through it. Control analysis looks at the source behind the content, and effect analysis at the traces left in the reader.

evidence-shannon.prompt: Which of the following is true of Shannon’s channel capacity result?
options: It shows he had built a code that removes noise completely.
It says that below capacity the error can be made as small as one likes; but it does not show how to construct good codes.
It applies only to telephone lines and also proves human communication.
It proves that channel capacity is a measure of meaning.
evidence-shannon.explain: The second option is correct: the result is a limit and a possibility claim; building good codes is a separate job (turbo-codes came forty-five years later). The first option comes from thinking noise can be removed; but noise limits the capacity. The third and fourth options carry the theory over to meaning and people; in 1956 Shannon left exactly that as an experimental question.

crit-linear.prompt: A set of lecture notes says “the Lasswell model is inadequate because it ignores feedback”. Which of the following is the most balanced response?
options: True; Lasswell had deliberately forbidden feedback.
False; feedback is clearly defined within the formula.

Partly: the formula does not mention feedback, but according to some authors the objection is aimed mostly at the boxes-and-arrows presentations drawn later; the list of questions does not exclude feedback.
This objection applies only to the Shannon–Weaver model and means nothing for Lasswell.
crit-linear.explain: The third option carries both the objection’s valid side (the formula does not mention feedback) and the defenders’ reasoning (the boxes-and-arrows presentations, not the list of questions itself). The first option attributes to Lasswell a prohibition he did not make; the second attributes to the formula an element it does not have; the fourth narrows the objection too much, because the feedback critique is made of Lasswell’s formula as well.

crit-caution.prompt: A student writes in an assignment: “Shannon proved that the human brain works like an ideal receiver.” According to Shannon’s 1956 editorial, what is the most accurate correction?
options: Correct; since the theory is mathematics it applies to humans with certainty.
That a human being acts in some situations like an ideal decoder is an experimental, not a mathematical, fact; it must be tested by experiments.
Shannon proved that a human being can never act like an ideal receiver.
This sentence could be written only about Weaver, not about Shannon.
crit-caution.explain: This is exactly what Shannon says in the editorial: a human being acting as an ideal decoder is an experimental fact. The first option falls for the ‘maths = applies with certainty’ shortcut; Shannon says that carrying the mathematical core to other fields is not as easy as translating words. The third option also attributes an unproven certainty: it was neither proved nor refuted, but left as a question to be asked.

crit-needle.prompt: True or false: Lasswell’s 1927 propaganda book also contains warnings that the effect of propaganda cannot be measured precisely and can be exaggerated by the defeated.
crit-needle.explain: True. The book’s ‘results’ chapter says that the precise effect of propaganda is largely a matter of surmise and that defeated countries exaggerate the influence of propaganda; the same chapter continues to count propaganda as a powerful instrument. The ‘Lasswell = unlimited effect’ association is built without reading the second half of the book.

today-digital.prompt: A corner of a QR code is smudged and the code is still read. In Shannon’s terms, what makes this possible?
options: The phone guessing the meaning of the code
Deliberately added redundancy (an error-correcting code)
The smudge not counting as noise
The QR code having infinite channel capacity
today-digital.explain: A QR code uses an error-correcting code that deliberately adds redundancy to the data; even if a smudge damages part of the code, the original data is rebuilt thanks to the redundancy. The first option is tempting because it looks as if ‘the phone understands’; but the system repairs a bit pattern, not a meaning. The third option reverses the definition of noise (the smudge is a distortion the source did not want); the fourth assumes infinite capacity, whereas every channel has a capacity.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question asks: “Which of the following is NOT one of Lasswell’s original three functions?” Which is the correct answer?
options: Surveillance of the environment
Correlating the parts of society in responding to the environment
Transmission of the social heritage
Entertainment
exam-patterns.explain: Entertainment is an item added to the list later and is generally attributed to Wright; Lasswell’s original list has three items: surveillance, correlation, transmission. This question tests the ‘fourth function’ trap: a student who has memorised a four-item list may know the first three options yet hesitate to mark the last as ‘not one’.

summary.prompt: True or false: Shannon’s theory measures how precisely the meaning of a message is understood by the receiver.
summary.explain: False. Shannon’s theory measures how accurately a message is carried and the choice among possible messages; meaning is kept outside the engineering problem. How precisely meaning is understood belongs to Weaver’s level B (semantic), and Shannon’s mathematics does not deal with this level directly.

quiz.prompt: Which attitude in the introduction of Shannon’s 1948 paper most clearly separates it from Lasswell’s formula?
options: Treating the semantic aspects of a message as irrelevant to the engineering problem
Putting effect as a single question
Treating communication only at the level of society
Not mentioning the channel at all
quiz.explain: Shannon accepts that messages may have meaning but treats this as irrelevant to the engineering problem; Lasswell’s questions put content and effect at the centre. It is Lasswell who puts effect as a single question (second option) and who thinks at the level of society (third option); and the channel is present in both models (the fourth option is wrong).

quiz.prompt: True or false: In 1948 Lasswell wrote four functions of communication: surveillance, correlation, transmission and entertainment.
quiz.explain: False. Lasswell’s list has three items: surveillance, correlation, transmission. Adding entertainment as a fourth function is generally attributed to Wright (1960); but the four-item list is often wrongly credited to Lasswell.

quiz.prompt: Match the elements of Shannon’s diagram with their counterparts in the telegram example.
pairs: The person choosing the message from among possible messages
The process that turns letters into a sequence of dots and dashes
The wire the signals travel over
Static on the line that the source did not want
The apparatus that turns the signals back into letters
quiz.explain: The source chooses, the transmitter encodes, the channel carries, noise is the distortion the source did not want, and the receiver does the inverse of the transmitter. The pair most often confused is transmitter and receiver: both ‘convert’, but in opposite directions.

quiz.prompt: Put the events in chronological order (oldest to newest).
items: The two parts of Shannon’s paper and the book carrying Lasswell’s chapter (1948)
quiz.explain: The order: 1928 Hartley, 1941 Shannon at Bell, 1948 Lasswell and Shannon, 1949 the book, 1956 the editorial, 1960 Wright. The most common mistake is putting the book (1949) before the paper (1948); the paper came out a year earlier in two parts.

quiz.text: According to Weaver, communication problems arise at three levels: the {{1}} problem is the question of how accurately the symbols are transmitted; the {{2}} problem is how precisely the transmitted symbols convey the desired meaning; and the {{3}} problem is how effectively the received meaning affects conduct in the desired way.

options: technical
semantic
effectiveness
effectiveness
technical
semantic
semantic
effectiveness
technical

quiz.explain: Level A is the technical problem (accurate transmission), level B is the semantic problem (meaning), level C is the effectiveness problem (conduct). Confusion usually arises between B and C: receiving the meaning correctly is one thing, changing behaviour another.

quiz.scenario: A municipality sets up an SMS warning system against flood risk. The team does two jobs: (a) testing that messages arrive without corruption, (b) measuring how many people left the area after a warning. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: Which of Weaver’s levels does job (a) belong to?
options: Technical (A)
Semantic (B)
Effectiveness (C)
parts.explain: A message arriving without corruption is the accurate transmission of symbols: the technical problem, level A. The semantic level looks at how the message is understood, and the effectiveness level at behaviour.

parts.prompt: Which of Lasswell’s fields of analysis does measurement (b) correspond to?
options: Control analysis
Content analysis
Effect analysis
parts.explain: Measuring what was done after a warning is the field of the ‘with what effect?’ question: effect analysis. Content analysis examines what the message says, and control analysis who sent it and under what conditions.

parts.prompt: Which of Lasswell’s three functions is the system’s reporting of the flood threat to the public an example of?
options: Surveillance of the environment
Correlation
Transmission of the social heritage
parts.explain: Reporting a threat is the surveillance function. Correlation coordinates the response of the parts of society (for example the municipality, the school and the public meeting on the same plan); transmission concerns the heritage passed between generations.

quiz.takeaway: The same system can be measured with two rulers: Weaver asks ‘was it carried correctly, was it understood, did it work?’; Lasswell asks ‘who, what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect?’ and ‘what job does it do for society?’.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is true of Lasswell’s 1927 propaganda book?
options: It counts propaganda as powerful but also writes that its precise effect is largely a matter of surmise.
It argues that propaganda has no effect at all.
It is the book that first used the term “hypodermic needle”.
It rests only on audience surveys.
quiz.explain: The book counts propaganda as one of the most powerful instruments of the modern world, but also writes that the precise measure of its effect is often guesswork. The second option is an opposite caricature. The phrase ‘hypodermic needle’ does not occur in the book; the third option attributes a label added later to the book itself. The book deals with the organisation, themes and results of war propaganda; audience surveys are not its subject.

quiz.prompt: What is the main message of Shannon’s 1956 editorial “The Bandwagon”?
options: A call for caution and rigour against applying information theory to other fields with enthusiasm and haste
That information theory explains all the social sciences
That information theory should now be abandoned
That meaning is an engineering problem
quiz.explain: Shannon writes that the theory had become a bandwagon, that applying it to other fields is not as easy as translating words, and that it demands hypotheses and experiments; he does not abandon the theory but goes on counting it a valuable tool. The second option is the exact opposite, the third is an extreme reading, and the fourth reverses Shannon’s starting attitude.

quiz.prompt: Compare a fair coin toss with tossing a rigged coin that lands heads 99 per cent of the time. According to Shannon’s measure, which has the higher entropy (greater uncertainty)?
options: The fair coin toss
The rigged coin toss
They are equal
The measure depends on the meaning of the coin
quiz.explain: With two equally likely options entropy takes its highest value (1 bit); as one becomes almost certain it approaches zero. The second option comes from the intuition ‘rigged = more information’; but the rigged coin gives the result almost in advance. The fourth option forgets that Shannon’s measure is independent of meaning.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Warren Weaver was Shannon’s co-worker at Bell Laboratories.
quiz.explain: False. Weaver headed the Rockefeller Foundation’s natural sciences division; he is the author of the essay that opened Shannon’s paper to the general reader. The ‘co-worker’ image comes from the joint name ‘Shannon–Weaver’.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best sums up the critique of the “linear transmission model”?
options: Communication is not only the carrying of a message; it also includes meaning, context and the sharing of a common world.
Communication consists only of noise.
The concept of the channel is entirely unnecessary.
Effect is an element of communication that can never be measured.
quiz.explain: The transmission critique (for example Carey’s ritual view) says communication is not only carrying but building shared meaning and a shared world. The other options are extreme claims no one defends; rejecting channel or effect as concepts is not what the objection is about.
